title: Gastroschisis
subject: Surgery
summary: Gastroschisis is a full‑thickness abdominal wall defect, usually right of the umbilical cord, with exposed bowel lacking a protective sac. It presents in newborns, often premature, and requires prompt surgical management to prevent infection and bowel damage.

sections.p: A full‑thickness defect of the anterior abdominal wall, typically to the right of a normal umbilical cord, through which loops of small and large intestine protrude without a covering sac.
b: No peritoneal sac; bowel is directly bathed in amniotic fluid
Usually isolated; major associated anomalies are rare (<10%)

sections.p: Severity is graded by the amount of bowel exteriorized and the presence of bowel wall changes (thickened, matted, peel).
b: Stage I: Minimal bowel, thin peel, primary closure possible
Stage II: Moderate bowel, thick peel, requires silo before closure
Stage III: Massive bowel, severe edema/ischemia, may need staged reduction and possible bowel resection

sections.p: Exact cause unknown; most accepted theory is a vascular disruption of the right omphalomesenteric artery early in gestation.
b: Ischemic disruption of right omphalomesenteric artery (most likely)
Rupture of a tiny omphalocele sac in utero
Maternal factors: young age, smoking, low socioeconomic status

sections.p: Newborn is delivered with visible loops of bowel protruding from the right of the umbilicus; the bowel appears thickened, matted and covered with a shaggy peel.
b: Visible, non‑encapsulated bowel outside abdomen
Prematurity or low birth weight in >70% of cases
Possible feeding intolerance, abdominal distension after birth

t.b: Confirms diagnosis; assesses amount of bowel and condition of peel
Shows gas pattern; helps detect associated atresia
Evaluates bowel wall thickness, detects intra‑abdominal anomalies
Prepares for possible transfusion during surgery
Detects dehydration, hypoglycaemia from fluid loss

sections.p: Complications arise from bowel exposure and impaired perfusion.
b: Severe bowel edema or ischemia → necrosis
Intestinal atresia or perforation
Sepsis from contaminated exposed bowel
Fluid‑electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycaemia

sections.p: Urgent protection of exposed bowel, stabilisation, then surgical reduction and closure.
b: Cover bowel with sterile, moist, non‑adhesive dressing (e.g., saline‑soaked gauze) to prevent drying and infection
IV fluids with dextrose and electrolytes; maintain normothermia
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin) – avoid nephrotoxic drugs if renal function uncertain
If primary closure possible, perform within first 24 h; otherwise place a silo for gradual reduction
Resect non‑viable bowel only when clearly necrotic; preserve length to avoid short‑bowel syndrome
Post‑operative ventilation if needed; monitor urine output and electrolytes

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on nutrition, growth and detection of late complications.
b: Early enteral feeding once bowel function returns; monitor for feeding intolerance
Growth monitoring; consider supplemental calories for premature infants
Surveillance for adhesive small‑bowel obstruction
Counselling on maternal risk factors (smoking cessation, optimal spacing) for future pregnancies
Omphalocele – covered by a peritoneal sac, central umbilical location, higher rate of chromosomal anomalies
Exomphalos minor – small omphalocele with sac, not a true gastroschisis

sections.p: Some investigations may appear normal despite serious disease.
b: Plain X‑ray may miss a short segment of atresia; clinical suspicion should prompt contrast study if possible
Normal serum electrolytes early on do not rule out rapid fluid loss; repeat labs frequently

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid increase in abdominal wall defect size
Signs of bowel necrosis (black, dusky bowel)
Severe abdominal distension with poor perfusion

faq.q: Why is gastroschisis more common in young mothers?
faq.a: Maternal age <20 is associated with vascular disruption and higher rates of smoking, both risk factors for the defect.

faq.q: Can gastroschisis close spontaneously before birth?
faq.a: No; the defect remains open, and the bowel stays exposed throughout gestation.

faq.q: What is the main difference between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
faq.a: Gastroschisis lacks a protective sac and is lateral to the cord; omphalocele has a sac and is midline.

exam: What immediate bedside steps do you take for a newborn with suspected gastroschisis? — Cover bowel with sterile moist dressing, start IV fluids with dextrose, give broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange urgent surgical review.
How does the presence of a thick, matted peel influence your surgical plan? — Indicates bowel edema; primary closure unlikely, so a silo is placed for staged reduction.
Which maternal risk factor is most strongly linked to gastroschisis and why? — Young maternal age (<20 y) due to higher likelihood of vascular disruption and smoking exposure.
What distinguishes gastroschisis from omphalocele on physical exam? — Absence of a covering sac and lateral (right‑side) location versus a central sac‑covered defect.
When is bowel resection indicated in gastroschisis? — Only when bowel is clearly non‑viable (black, no peristalsis, absent arterial pulsation) to avoid unnecessary loss of length.

Why are broad‑spectrum antibiotics started before surgery, and which agents are preferred in low‑resource settings? — To prevent sepsis from contaminated exposed bowel; ampicillin plus gentamicin is effective and widely available.
What long‑term complication should you monitor for after successful closure? — Adhesive small‑bowel obstruction and growth failure due to possible short‑bowel syndrome.
If an X‑ray is unavailable, how can you assess for associated intestinal atresia? — Use bedside ultrasound to look for dilated loops and absent peristalsis, and monitor feeding tolerance closely.
